summary: A satirical local-news piece mocks the City Council's new zoning laws, announced after a marathon meeting on November 19, 2023, which were billed as streamlining housing development. Critics and developers say the rules add red tape, including conditional use permits, setback requirements, an aesthetic review committee and a new Civic Beautification Reconnaissance Division. The article ends by predicting continued friction between council and developers, with paperwork prevailing over progress.
one_line: A satirical take on the City Council's new zoning laws, which promise easier housing development but pile on permits, committees and bureaucracy.
key_facts: The City Council announced new zoning laws after a marathon meeting on November 19, 2023.
Council Member James "Jimbo" McScroops spearheaded the new zoning regulations.
The laws are said to promote varied housing types, from high-rises to "hobbit holes".

The fine print includes conditional use permits, setback requirements, and an aesthetic review committee, said to be made up of retired art teachers and one person devoted to neighborhood Halloween decorations.
The council created the Civic Beautification Reconnaissance Division (CBRD) to ensure new structures contribute positively to the city's aesthetic.
Rachel Rendertown, self-appointed head of CBRD and a known enthusiast of brutalist birdhouses, said the division is crucial for guarding the cityscape against "architectural travesties".
McScroops said of the new laws: "these new laws are going to change the game".
Local developer Wendy Walls said: "It's like they want us to jump through hoops, but the hoops are on fire, and they keep moving the hoops."
Developer Arthur "Artie" Brickman said project timelines have "more padding than a sumo wrestler's suit" and now lists personalized pens for required signatures as line items in his quotes.
The council, with little opposition, approved a new task force to "expedite the expediting process".
The article frames the intent to tackle housing shortages and rising rents as noble but says the red tape could suffocate housing development.
A city spokesperson, asked about the chilly development climate, offered a chuckle reminiscent of "Let them eat cake".
